newsitem.title: KENYA: Tanzania sees sharp drop in coffee production.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania sees sharp drop in coffee production.

text.p: Tanzanian coffee authorities forecast a sharp fall in coffee production in 1997/98 (October/September) with prices continuing to rise due to tight domestic and global supplies.

Njelu Kasaka, Tanzania's deputy minister for agriculture and co-operatives, told Reuters 1997/98 output was estimated at 30,000 to 35,000 tonnes compared to 41,000 in 1996/97 and around 53,000 tonnes in 1995/96.
The figure would be the lowest for almost a decade.
Kasaka said in an interview seasonal long rains that arrived late in March ending a six-month drought were too late for the new crop, which would now be significantly smaller.
Tanzania Coffee Board Public Relations Manager Damian Salla said drought had caused production to decline but he did not see it dropping as low as the minister's forecast.

Traders in the northern coffee town of Moshi said an expected fall in production of good quality coffee from the main Mount Kilimanjaro area would force auction prices higher in the second half of calendar 1997.
Jeremy Lefroy, managing director at leading traders African Coffee Company, said prices had doubled in the first half of the calendar year, partly on global shortages.

Good quality grades AA and AB's sold at an average $260 per 50-kg at Tanzania's last auction on May 15 compared to $130 at the beginning of the year. Tanzania holds two coffee auctions a month in Moshi.
Another trader said "We will see very high prices ...in line with the international market and simply because the competition will be very stiff."

Other traders said that although they were now selling lower quality coffees -- leftovers from the main crop -- there was continued demand and roasters were buying as much coffee as they could lay their hands on.
"We have Japanese roasters who are just buying because they know the new crop will be smaller," one trader noted.
The new crop from the northern Kilimanjaro area is expected around June-July while coffee from further south will become available from August.
Kasaka said Tanzania planned to raise production by renewing old plants, improving husbandry and expanding into new regions.
"In the northern parts of the country, mainly Kilimanjaro and Arusha regions, land is increasingly becoming scarce due to population density and competition with other crops.
"Some people are uprooting coffee trees in favour of other crops like tomatoes and beans and some are turning to flower growing," he said.

Kasaka said his department sent field officers to preach the coffee gospel in the southern highlands of Iringa, Mbeya and Ruvuma where climate was favourable and there was plenty of land, adding "We hope in the next three years coffee output will increase to around 80,000 tonnes."

He said the European Union was backing Tanzania's coffee development programmes and had provided cash to compensate farmers for the 1992/93 period when global prices were low and for generation of quality seedlings. Around 420,000 farmers will gain from EU funds. --Nairobi Newsroom ++254-2 330-261.
